difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE - one concept with 2-3 routine steps: rebuild a 7-node binary tree from its pre-order and in-order traversals, then derive its post-order and read off the child structure. All four statements follow from the same reconstructed tree, so no level bump applies; about 1.5 minutes.
stem:
You are given the following Pre-order and In-order traversals of a Binary Tree T with nodes `E`, `F`, `G`, `P`, `Q`, `R`, `S`.

Pre-order: `P` `Q` `S` `E` `R` `F` `G`

In-order: `S` `Q` `E` `P` `F` `R` `G`

Which of the following statements is/are true about the Binary Tree T?

options.label: A
options.text: Node `P` is the root of T

options.label: B
options.text:
The Post-order traversal of T is:

`S` `E` `Q` `F` `G` `R` `P`

options.label: D
options.text: The left subtree of node `R` contains the node `G`

solution.quick:
Pre-order starts with the root, so the root is P. In-order splits at P into left {S, Q, E} and right {F, R, G}. Recursing gives Q with children S (left) and E (right), and R with children F (left) and G (right).

The tree is P(Q(S, E), R(F, G)), with post-order S E Q F G R P. So (A) and (B) are true, (C) is false (Q has two children), and (D) is false (G is R's right child). **(A), (B)**

steps.title: Reconstruction rule
steps.body:
For a binary tree with distinct labels:

1. The **first** node of the pre-order sequence is the root.
2. Find that root in the in-order sequence. Everything to its left forms the left subtree and everything to its right forms the right subtree.
3. If the left subtree has $k$ nodes, the next $k$ pre-order entries after the root belong to the left subtree and the rest to the right subtree. Recurse on each part.

steps.title: Root and first split
steps.body:
- Pre-order: **P** Q S E R F G, so the root is **P**.
- In-order: S Q E | **P** | F R G, so the left subtree is $\{S, Q, E\}$ (3 nodes) and the right subtree is $\{F, R, G\}$ (3 nodes).
- Split the rest of the pre-order accordingly. The left part is Q S E (next 3 entries) and the right part is R F G (last 3 entries).

steps.title: Left and right subtrees
steps.body:
**Left subtree:** pre-order Q S E, in-order S Q E.

- Root **Q** (first in pre-order). In the in-order, S is left of Q and E is right of Q.
- So Q has left child **S** and right child **E**.

**Right subtree:** pre-order R F G, in-order F R G.

- Root **R**. In the in-order, F is left of R and G is right of R.
- So R has left child **F** and right child **G**.

The reconstructed tree T:

```text
        P
      /   \
     Q     R
    / \   / \
   S   E F   G
```

Check: the in-order of this tree is S Q E P F R G, which matches the given sequence.

steps.title: Post-order traversal
steps.body:
Post-order visits left subtree, then right subtree, then the root:

$$
\text{post}(T) = \text{post}(Q\text{-subtree}) \;\|\; \text{post}(R\text{-subtree}) \;\|\; P = (S, E, Q) \;\|\; (F, G, R) \;\|\; P.
$$

Here $\|$ denotes concatenation. So the post-order is **S E Q F G R P**.

steps.title: Evaluate each statement
steps.body:
| Statement | From the tree | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (A) P is the root | P is first in pre-order | true |
| (B) Post-order is S E Q F G R P | Computed: S E Q F G R P | true |
| (C) Q has only one child | Q has two children, S and E | false |
| (D) Left subtree of R contains G | R's left subtree is only F, and G is its right child | false |

**Answer: (A), (B).**

solution.teaching:
**The three depth-first traversals.** Each visits the root $N$, its left subtree $L$ and its right subtree $R$, applying the same rule recursively inside each subtree. They differ only in *when* the root is visited:

- **Pre-order:** $N, L, R$. The root comes **first**.
- **In-order:** $L, N, R$. The root sits **between** its two subtrees.
- **Post-order:** $L, R, N$. The root comes **last**.

**Why pre-order + in-order pins down the tree.** Pre-order tells you *which* node is the root. In-order then tells you *which nodes go left and which go right*, because everything before the root in in-order lies in its left subtree. The number of nodes on the left tells you how to cut the rest of the pre-order sequence. Applying this recursively fixes every node's position, so with distinct labels the tree is unique. The same works with post-order + in-order (the root is then the *last* post-order entry). Pre-order + post-order alone is not enough in general: if a node has a single child, the two sequences cannot tell whether that child is on the left or the right.

**A useful sanity check.** Once the tree is rebuilt, regenerate the in-order sequence from it and compare it with the given one. For a post-order answer, check that it ends with the root and that the left subtree's nodes form one contiguous block ending with the left child's root.

**Back to this question.** P is the root, and the in-order splits it 3 | 3. Each half splits 1 | 1 again, so T is the perfect binary tree P(Q(S, E), R(F, G)). Reading it off: post-order S E Q F G R P (B true), P is the root (A true), Q has two children (C false), and G is R's right child (D false).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Pre-order visits the root first, and the pre-order sequence begins with P. So P is the root.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Post-order of the rebuilt tree is (S, E, Q) from Q's subtree, then (F, G, R) from R's subtree, then P, giving S E Q F G R P, exactly as stated.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: In the in-order sequence S Q E, S lies left of Q and E lies right of Q. So Q has **two** children, S (left) and E (right).

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: In the in-order sequence F R G, G lies to the **right** of R. So G is R's right child, and R's left subtree contains only F.

solution.shortcut: The in-order splits at P into 3 | 3, and each block of three splits at its pre-order root (Q, then R) into 1 | 1. So T is the perfect tree P(Q(S, E), R(F, G)). Each of Q and R has two leaf children, so the post-order is simply (left leaf, right leaf, parent) for each side, then the root: S E Q, F G R, P.
solution.commonTrap: Reading parent–child links straight off the pre-order sequence. Seeing "Q S E" consecutively, a student may think S is Q's only child and E is S's child, and mark (C). The in-order S Q E shows that S and E sit on opposite sides of Q. Another slip is reversing the pre-order to get a "post-order" (G F R E S Q P). Post-order is left–right–root, which is not the reverse of root–left–right.
